articles.title: La Bola Negra: this deeply moving cinematic homage to Lorca is part of his queer legacy
articles.author: Santiago Fouz Hernández, Professor in the School of Modern Languages and Cultures, Durham University
paras: Directed by legendary Spanish film-making duo Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – also known as “Los Javis” – La Bola Negra (The Black Ball) is Spain’s big hope for next year’s Oscars.

The film reimagines the unfinished 1936 work of the same name by the Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca (1898-1936), based on the only four existing pages. It would have been Lorca’s first play with a gay protagonist.

La bola negra is also co-written by Los Javis in collaboration with queer playwright Alberto Conejero, author of the original play La Piedra Oscura (The Dark Stone, 2013) on which the film is also partly based.

The film’s title refers to Lorca’s original story, in which Carlos, a young gay man (Milo Quifes) tries and fails to join a private club due to rumours about his sexuality. The selection committee votes in secret, using white and black balls. The black ones represent rejection – hence the term “blackballed” – and, implicitly, social exclusion.

Los Javis first became well known for three major streaming series: the hilarious Paquita Salas (Netflix 2020), a tragicomic story about a has-been talent agent; Veneno (HBO Max, 2020), based on the life of a trans sex worker who became a national celebrity in 1990s Spain; and the ambitious religious musical drama La Mesías (MUBI, 2023).

It is hard to believe that La Bola Negra is only their second feature, after La llamada (Holy Camp, 2017), their hugely successful musical about a lesbian romance. This new film is a significant leap in scale, production values and global reach.

After La Bola Negra’s triumph at Cannes, where Los Javis won best direction, the film also won audience awards at San Sebastián, Toronto and London, drawing full houses on the festival circuit. It also quickly became a social media phenomenon and has been acquired by Netflix.
Federico García Lorca and queer history
Lorca, considered Spain’s most influential 20th-century poet and playwright, was executed by firing squad in 1936, at the start of the Spanish civil war, because of his politics and sexuality.

In the film, Lorca’s unfinished text is a seed that grows and expands into the 21st century, pausing at three moments in Spain’s history: the second republic in 1932, the civil war in 1937, and contemporary Spain in 2017, taking in three gay stories.

In the second story, based on Conejero’s play, Lorca’s real-life lover Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau) is a Republican prisoner of war. He develops a fleeting platonic infatuation for his Nationalist guard, Sebastián, played brilliantly by popular singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente in his first acting role.

Their connection becomes part of a complex chain of relationships and revelations that carries the story – and queer history – forward, aided by an enveloping score by Raül Refree and exquisite cinematography by Gris Jordana.

Lorca’s legacy runs through the film, explicitly through his unfinished play, his homoerotic sketches, and even his presence depicted in a small cameo (Alberto Cortés). More implicitly, it is evoked through the dramatic Spanish settings and the depiction of motherhood, a subject he examined extensively in his work.

Lola Dueñas gives a remarkable supporting performance as Teresa, a troubled single mother. Penélope Cruz’s stellar performance as a glamorous cabaret singer includes one of the film’s most memorable lines, while Glenn Close plays an American Lorca scholar entirely in Spanish.

The film is packed with queer imagery across time. These range from a war-torn statue of the persecuted Saint Sebastian, who has become a contemporary queer-icon, to hypermasculine sailor figures reminiscent of German film-maker Rainer Werner Fassbinder’s classic homoerotic film Querelle, to the unmistakable gay dating app Grindr.

Shot on 35mm film, La Bola Negra seamlessly combines moments of great drama and intense intimacy in relatively small spaces that contrast with landscapes of epic proportions. Jordana’s lush cinematography gives the movie a consistent look throughout, while creating a distinctive ambience for each of the three story parts.

The film’s queer gaze embraces both ideals of masculinity and body diversity. Alongside the taut bodies of the characters played by heartthrobs Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente, the protagonist of the final section is Alberto, a larger-bodied gay man played by Carlos González. Famous for his queer roles in streaming hits such as Veneno (2020), and Mariliendre (Fag Hag, 2025), González delivers another standout performance, while adding important elements of body and sex positivity to the story.

Queer people have long been excluded from official histories: ignored, silenced or presented in ways that obscure their sexuality. In repressive societies, invisibility is a matter of survival, shaped by internalised homophobia and imposed closets. La Bola Negra makes that history visible, while celebrating the role queer people play in shaping culture: Lorca as a playwright, Sebastián as a musician, Alberto as a queer historian.

That reclamation has resonance in today’s Spain, a country often associated with LGBTQ+ progress. The third country in the world to legalise same-sex marriage in 2005, Spain currently ranks first in Europe on the 2026 Rainbow Map for legal rights and protections, yet the political climate feels increasingly uncertain.

Francoist and fascist nostalgia is finding new audiences through social media, even among young people, and the possibility of a conservative and far-right coalition hangs over Spain’s general election on November 29. As cultural historian Nicholas Manganas has argued, the film’s return to Spain’s past feels strikingly connected to the present.

Lorca’s remains are still believed to lie in an unmarked mass grave in his native province of Granada. His unfinished manuscript, however, survives as a symbol of queer legacy and inheritance. In the film, its pages become a baton passed across generations. But they are also an emblem of reparation for the queer shame, represented in the film by the black ball of the title, and its symbolic weight in Lorca’s original 1936 story.

By bringing the Spanish poet and playwright’s story back to life through an predominantly queer cast in a production that is heavy with queer iconography, Los Javis make La Bola Negra part of the very legacy their film seeks to reclaim.
Santiago Fouz Hernández receives funding from the British Academy. He is affiliated with the Spanish Government as Honorary Vice Consul of Spain for the North East and Cumbria.

articles.title: What C.S. Lewis said about Narnia’s most famous character: the Jesus-like lion Aslan
articles.author: Christopher A. Snyder, PhD, Professor of History, Mississippi State University
paras: As Netflix teases glimpses of Greta Gerwig’s newest project, an adaptation of C.S. Lewis’ novel “The Magician’s Nephew,” many Narnia fans are worried. In particular, there’s been online chatter about the new film’s depiction of the great lion Aslan: Will he really look like David Bowie, with the voice of Meryl Streep?

For many readers, Aslan is not just a literary character, nor an ordinary hero: He is a representation of Jesus. Aslan sings the entire world of Narnia into existence and performs Christ-like acts throughout Lewis’ “Chronicles of Narnia,” which have sold over 120 million copies worldwide since the series’ publication in the 1950s.

As a scholar of medieval history and literature, I’ve taught and written about Lewis and “Lord of the Rings” author J.R.R. Tolkien, who were close friends and colleagues for more than 30 years. Lewis himself was a medievalist at Oxford, and both of their popular literary series are steeped in their knowledge of medieval languages, literature, mythology and theology.
Both authors acknowledged the ethical and religious themes of their fiction. Yet Lewis rejected the idea that “The Chronicles” were simply an allegory.

“The Magician’s Nephew,” published in 1955, was actually the last book in the series to be completed. Yet it serves as a prequel, narrating the creation of Narnia and the first appearance of its legitimate ruler, Aslan – the Turkish word for “lion.”

Later in the series, Aslan sacrifices himself to save a young British boy, Edmund Pevensie, from the White Witch, Jadis. Aslan is resurrected through his knowledge of “deeper magic,” and royal power passes to the four Pevensie children.

Christian readers have long seen the series as an imaginative retelling of events from the Gospels, intended for children but offering much to adult readers as well. Critics like Philip Pullman, who wrote the 1990s fantasy trilogy “His Dark Materials,” have denounced “The Chronicles” as religious “propaganda.”

Adding to the book’s religious appeal was Lewis’ own very public faith. An atheist since his youth, he returned to worshipping in the Church of England after a famous late-night conversation with Tolkien in September 1931.

The two English professors had bonded over their interest in Norse myths, which Lewis called beautiful “lies breathed through silver.” For the devoutly Catholic Tolkien, however, ancient myths pointed to truths, not lies, and ultimately to the Gospels. He and other Christian friends at Oxford helped Lewis come to accept Christianity as the “true myth.”

Almost immediately, Lewis began writing Christian apologetics, intellectual defenses of his faith, as well as fiction infused with Christian symbolism and theology. In 1947, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine – well on his way to becoming arguably the most famous Christian apologist of the 20th century.
But what did Lewis himself say about Aslan?
His letters and scholarly work indicate that “The Chronicles” were not meant to be allegorical. In other words, Aslan was not simply a stand-in for Jesus, and the series was not an extended metaphor.
Rather, Lewis called the books “supposals:” a way of asking, “What if?”

Aslan gives “an imaginary answer to the question, ‘What might Christ become like if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” Lewis wrote in a 1958 letter. “This is not allegory at all.”

Neither Lewis nor Tolkien approved of easy allegorical readings of their fiction. Both professors argued that imaginative literature was not simply the product of the author and their time, a sealed treasure waiting for a biographical key to unlock its meaning.

And both men knew formal allegory quite well. Lewis’ 1936 book “The Allegory of Love” established his reputation as a critic of medieval and Renaissance literature. His 1933 novel “The Pilgrim’s Regress” was an allegorical exploration of his own conversion, with characters that personified various abstract concepts and ideologies.

Tolkien wrote the allegorical short story “Leaf by Niggle” as a way to explore his own doubts about ever finishing “The Lord of the Rings.” Like his earlier novel “The Hobbit,” “The Lord of the Rings” only came to fruition through Lewis’ constant encouragement.

Narnia came to Lewis’ mind in bits and pieces. During World War II, when he took young evacuees from bombed cities into his home, a lion had haunted his dreams. A few other mental pictures came to him – a faun carrying packages, a lamppost in the snow – and he began writing. Aslan “just insisted on behaving in His own way,” Lewis later wrote to one schoolgirl.

“The Chronicles” were not an allegory, he insisted, but symbolic. As he described in “The Allegory of Love,” “The symbolist leaves the given [facts] to find that which is more real.” Myth and symbols can, if used correctly, point to philosophical or theological truths more effectively than realistic fiction, making their created worlds feel more real.

For fans of “The Chronicles,” Narnia feels “real” in this sense – an escape to truth, rather than an escape from truth. Adapting these stories to film, however, always runs the risk of moving further away from what Lewis captured so brilliantly in his prose.

In 2018, the author’s estate sold Netflix the rights to adapt the book series to screen, and Gerwig was later tapped to write and direct at least two Narnia films. Douglas Gresham, one of Lewis’ stepsons, has an executive producer credit on “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” and has generally been enthusiastic about the project.

Gerwig herself has expressed her “reverence” for Lewis’ work. “It was the book of my childhood,” she said at a press event in 2024. “It was the book series that I loved, and I lived through, and I spent so much time imagining myself inside of Narnia.”

Intense scrutiny of the project should surprise no one. As with her film “Little Women,” Gerwig is adapting a beloved novel. And this time, it is a novel written by a very public atheist-turned-Christian whose works have inspired the faith of countless others. Still, her “Magician’s Nephew” should not be judged by a trailer and a handful of interviews.

Lewis likely never expected that “The Chronicles” would turn into a live-action film, but he did believe in the power of imaginative art – whether ancient, medieval or modern – to move one toward truth. The virtues Faith, Hope, Charity and Prudence are frequently depicted in the medieval and Renaissance literature that Lewis loved and taught. Fans and filmmaker alike might benefit from remembering these virtues as well.

articles.title: AI won’t ever make a historically accurate film – but it could help archaeology create better stories
articles.author: Stephan Blum, Research Associate, Institute for Prehistory and Early History and Medieval Archaeology, University of Tübingen
paras: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticised for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story “historically accurate and true to the art of Homer” at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.
On October 23, the platform posted the first seven minutes.

As archaeologists and art historians, we’re not here to review the film for its artistic quality or even its historic accuracy. Instead, we’re here to point out the real problem with the whole endeavour: the promise of historical accuracy failed before the first frame was even rendered.

Contrary to what many of you might assume, as historians we think Musk’s underlying idea – bringing together everything archaeology and history have to offer and using AI as a tool to explore and work with that knowledge – is a genuinely exciting one. We see considerable potential in that approach: a system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar can hold in mind, such as how ceramic styles spread. The problem is turning that into a film that claims to be historically accurate.
Any attempt to produce a complete, coherent visual narrative would inevitably require AI to go beyond the evidence and invent what we do not know.

Archaeology is inevitably working with a fragmentary record: only a tiny proportion of the past survives in the ground, and only a fraction of that is ever excavated. For instance, open the boxes in the Troy depot and you’ll find spindle whorls and loom weights; however, you won’t find the cloth they made. Everyone at Troy wore textiles but the textiles are gone.

So, like the textiles, everything that cannot be recovered directly from the archaeological record has to be interpreted and explained through hypotheses, however well-founded they may be scientifically. There will always be gaps, uncertainties and competing interpretations.
AI, by design, would inevitably fill these gaps.

Suppose Grok Imagine was given everything the Troy Project holds: a century and a half of excavation, thousands of plans, pottery drawings and photographs, plus the small-finds catalogue. It would generate connections, details and entire scenarios where the historical and archaeological evidence offers no firm answers.
Generative AI is built to produce complete images, even when there are visible gaps. These gaps are often filled with influence from other existing media like film sets, games, paintings.

This is precisely where the problem lies: additions by AI may be plausible, even convincing. Some sceptical reviewers concede that some of those seven minutes pass for real. But convincing is not accurate, and the space between the two is where archaeology lives.

The Odyssey is also an interesting target for accuracy. It’s a poor witness to the past: shaped centuries after the palaces its about fell, it is a palimpsest of Mycenaean memory and iron age worldview – not a snapshot. Odysseus, Helen and Circe are not people archaeology could confirm. However, there is a lot of creative media about the world these characters are believed to have inhabited.

Back to those textiles. A model trained on that record would inherit our ignorance along with our knowledge. It will hallucinate or imagine because it must paint every pixel. It will draw on all the evidence, media and more connected to the themes and history to render a finished cloak, dyed and draped. This rendering will look like a convincingly accurate garment where the honest research answer is “fibre known, colour unknown”.
What survives is not what happened

None of this makes AI useless. A system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar could see – such as how ceramic styles spread. But every such pattern would first be a pattern in the record, not a picture of the past.

A genuinely archaeological AI would do what generative AI rarely does: show its uncertainty as clearly as its confidence. Take armour. Only fragments survive at Troy. Where evidence permits several reconstructions, it would show several rather than present one confident, definitive option. Where only fragments survive, it would show only the fragments. And where the evidence runs out, it would say so, clearly marking what is documented, what is inferred and what is merely plausible.

This approach to rendering possibilities is close to what the London Charter (2009) and the Seville Principles (2011), two international guidelines for virtual reconstructions of heritage, have long demanded: transparency rather than smoothing.

Which world gets reconstructed is also a choice. Troy spans phases centuries apart, and Mycenaean palaces differed from Hittite cities: there is no single “bronze age”. The record can support a conflict at Troy; it cannot establish Homer’s Trojan war as one event. However, an AI model picks one Troy and never mentions the choice.

The film will likely be forgotten within a news cycle or two; what remains is the method. The most accurate Odyssey would not be the most definitive or confident one; it would end where we began: on the boxes of whorls and weights, and the empty space where the cloth should be.
Historical accuracy does not mean filling every gap. It means showing where the gaps are.

articles.title: Four ways thinking like a strategist can make you a better padel player
articles.author: Veselina Stoyanova, Associate Professor in Strategy & International Management, University of Birmingham
paras: As an avid tennis player, I never imagined an injury would lead me to discover a new sport. But just a few months ago, forced to take a break from tennis, I picked up a padel racket for the first time. I assumed that years of playing tennis would give me a head start; after all, how different could two racket sports really be? To my surprise, the answer was “very.”

Padel, which originated in Mexico in the late 1960s, is an enclosed-court racket sport typically played in doubles. Combining elements of squash and tennis, it uses solid, stringless bats, lower-compression balls and glass or mesh walls off which the ball can rebound. While it has long been a sporting obsession in Spain and Latin America, its explosive global growth has recently made it the fastest-growing racket sport worldwide.

While tennis and padel share many technical similarities, they require somewhat different ways of thinking. I soon discovered that some of my tennis instincts were actually holding me back. Hitting harder wasn’t always the answer. Attacking too early often left me exposed, while patience, positioning, and anticipating my opponents’ next move proved far more valuable than a powerful shot.

That experience made me curious about something beyond court technique. As a researcher in strategic management, I focus on how people and organisations navigate uncertainty, allocate limited resources and make decisions to gain a competitive advantage. I quickly began to recognise these exact same challenges on the padel court.

What if, I wondered, the secret to becoming a better padel player isn’t simply learning to hit the ball better, but learning to think more strategically? Here are four ways thinking like a strategist can help you level up your padel game:
1. Consider yourself a resource orchestrator, not a player

According to resource orchestration theory, which emphasises how managers organise, combine and deploy resources to create value, success depends not simply on the resources you possess, but on how effectively you orchestrate them.

We can apply this directly to padel. For example, if your partner has an exceptional volley, try to create opportunities for them to use it. Before starting a match, discuss your individual strengths with your partner and plan how best to combine them. In fact, what you initially view as a resource constraint can often be turned to your advantage.
2. Train your attention, not just your shots

In both business and padel, your strategic mindset starts with where you focus your attention. The real power of training your attention is cumulative. During each game, choose one specific aspect to focus on closely: whether that is your opponents’ bandeja (a defensive overhead shot) or their footwork and movement.
After several games, your observations will accumulate into strategic insight. This accumulated knowledge allows you to anticipate your opponents’ moves rather than simply react to them.
3. Play the opponent in front of you, not the one in your head
To increase your odds of winning, try to reflect on and challenge your assumptions about your opponents and how you judge their moves on the padel court.

We often rely on first impressions about competitors, which can distort our judgement and affect our play and decisions. Instead, view your assumptions as hypotheses to be tested based on your opponents’ next shots, rather than as concrete truth.
4. Thinking backwards can lead you further forward
Instead of trying to assume your opponents’ next move, practice backward reasoning.
Imagine a situation where your opponents are dominating the net. Try not to assume their next move, but to influence the choices they make next.

To develop a strategic mindset and improve your padel practice, define your desired outcome and work backwards, identifying the decisions that will help you achieve it. Strategic management means that, rather than simply reacting to your opponents’ next moves, you actively consider how your own actions can influence their next shot.

To play strategically, stop asking yourself “Where should I hit the ball next?” and start asking “What position do I want to be in two shots from now, and how can my next shot help me get there?” By thinking backward from the outcome you want to create, you transition from reactive play to tactical planning.

For instance, if your opponents are dominating the net, your immediate goal isn’t to hit an instant winner, but to force them out of their attacking position. Hitting a soft drop or deep lob buys you time, surrenders their net advantage and sets up a favourable position to control the point on your next turn.

To become a better player in padel, tennis, or any racket sport, the smartest way to win a point is often to out-think rather than out-play your opponent. Next time you’re on the court, remember that your strategic mindset is a skill you can train – just like your forehand, volley, or bandeja.

articles.title: The John Lewis Christmas ad captures the deep need for grandmothers
articles.author: Helen Minnis, Professor of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Glasgow
paras: Like many of us, I always enjoy the John Lewis Christmas advert and 2026 is no different. This year, I love the fact that the star of the show is a grandmother.

Feeling disconnected from her visiting grandchildren and ready to resort to cash in envelopes for Christmas, Gloria (Kristin Scott Thomas) is scolded by her childhood toy dog Pickles, who comes to life and whisks her on a whirlwind London TukTuk ride. Inspired, Gloria transforms her home office into a glittering, disco-lit “gran cave”, bridging the generation gap by sharing her sense of wonder with her grandchildren.

We can’t all have grandmothers as chic as Gloria, but many of us were lucky enough to have grans who loved us just as much — and we probably took them as much for granted. I suspect many grans feel like an old-fashioned back boiler, half-invisible in the background, but warming the family without anyone noticing. Sociologists often refer to this as “kinkeeping”: the often unacknowledged emotional and practical groundwork that holds intergenerational families together, but is all too easily taken for granted.

Those grandparents lucky enough to see their grandchildren on a regular basis, and who get to be involved socially and emotionally in their lives, feel less lonely and tend to live healthier lives. Sadly though, many feel devalued by the younger generation.

Gran’s alliance with Pickles helps her to rediscover the real Gloria. The person who can lean her head back into the headrest of a fantasy shocking-pink super-chariot, and feel the wind in her hair as it whizzes her through the Christmas fairy-lit streets. The Gloria that is silly enough to spend her Christmas savings on glittery spangles. The Gloria that hasn’t forgotten how to dance. This is the gran that the children love.

This year’s John Lewis ad is a reminder that families are not just made up of mum, dad and 2.4 children. Humans are different from many of our ape cousins. We are “cooperative breeders”. This means we tend to have children in quick succession and, because human babies are unusually dependent compared to other baby apes, parents need help from other adults.

Across evolution, it seems that human parents drew in the help of “alloparents” – most often grandmothers but also grandfathers, aunties, uncles and cousins – to help with childcare. This was wonderful for the human species as children learned from a wide range of fascinating adults.

In many parts of the world, children live every day of the year surrounded by family members who can lift the load off parents and take their share of bringing up the kids. But the John Lewis advert is a reminder that many British families are nuclear. In these families, children grow up separated from grandparents, so that grans and granddads are left trying to reach out and create a Christmas relationship that in other parts of the world they might have all year round.

Research has shown that grandmothers can help reduce the risk of mothers getting depressed after a new baby is born; that having a gran living in the home can reduce the chances of a child needing to go to casualty after an accident; that grandmothers who help with childcare are good for children’s mental health and development.

Every year, festive ads tap into something we clearly miss: the chaotic, comforting warmth of a bigger family circle. Modern routines and long distances often leave grandparents sidelined until the holidays roll around. Yet as the science shows, being closely involved in each other’s lives protects grandparents against isolation and helps kids flourish.

Finding ways to keep that spark alive beyond December means more than finding the perfect presents. It’s about making room for the shared laughter, silliness and connection that both generations actually thrive on.
Helen Minnis receives funding from UKRI and NIHR. She is affiliated with the University of Glasgow.

articles.title: What makes music truly ‘Russian’? The forgotten debate between Tchaikovsky and his star pupil
articles.author: Stacy Olive Jarvis, PhD Candidate in in Musicology, University of Birmingham
paras: What makes a piece of music Russian? A folk tune, a church melody, or simply the fact that the composer was born in Russia? For 19th-century composer Sergei Taneyev (1856-1915), the answer was complicated. He wanted Russian composers to develop a musical voice of their own. But he believed they could do so by learning from composers elsewhere in Europe.

By the time Taneyev began his career, the world of classical music in Russia was expanding. Musical life, which had previously been centred on the imperial court and aristocratic families, increasingly came to include public concerts and new institutions for training professional musicians. Conservatoires opened in St Petersburg in 1862 and in Moscow in 1866, where teaching methods developed in various European countries were employed.

However, musicians’ views on how the Russian tradition should develop differed. Tchaikovsky was one of the first graduates of the St Petersburg Conservatoire. At the same time, a group known as “The Five” – César Cui, Aleksandr Borodin, Mily Balakirev, Modest Mussorgsky and Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov – drew on folk songs, Russian history and folk legends in their quest to forge a distinctive national style.
The question at stake was how Russian composers could create their own tradition while drawing on established European musical culture.

November 2026 marks 170 years since Taneyev’s birth. This anniversary offers a chance to revisit an argument with his former teacher, Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840-1893), over a question that still shapes how we listen: how much does a national identity label actually tell us about music?

Taneyev was closely connected to some of the best-known names in Russian classical music. He studied with Tchaikovsky, later taught Rachmaninoff and Scriabin, and directed the Moscow Conservatory between 1885 and 1889.

In my research on Tchaikovsky’s operas, I have explored how his music brought Saint Petersburg to life as a Russian city shaped by European culture. In his opera Eugene Onegin (based on the novel by Alexander Pushkin), elegant ballroom dances evoke the capital’s aristocratic society, contrasting with the rural world of the earlier scenes.
But Tchaikovsky and Taneyev argued over how drawing on European traditions could help composers develop a distinctively Russian voice.

Taneyev was troubled by the direction Russian music might take. He thought composers needed to do more than place Russian folk tunes inside the kinds of pieces already familiar from European concert halls.
Instead, they should examine how earlier European composers had turned folk songs and church melodies into complex works. Could Russian musicians do something similar with their own songs?

That meant studying counterpoint: the art of combining different melodies so that each remains distinct while working with the others. Bach was an important model. For Taneyev, learning these techniques could help a composer create music with a recognisably Russian character.

Education was part of the plan. Taneyev argued that Russian songs should become a foundation of musical training. Composers would learn their craft through melodies connected to their own surroundings, while drawing on knowledge built up elsewhere.
Tchaikovsky was sceptical. In their 1880 correspondence, he questioned whether Russian music could be separated from European music in the way his pupil proposed.
Taneyev explained his position through an image. European music was a tree that had grown over centuries from folk and church melodies. Russian melodies were seeds from which another tree might grow.

Russian composers therefore had a choice. They could help the existing European tree grow, or cultivate something of their own. Crucially, Taneyev did not want musicians to turn their backs on Europe. Its history could show them how to proceed. Studying another culture’s achievements could help them develop their own.

Tchaikovsky challenged the comparison. Why treat European music as a single tree? French, German and Italian music already had different characters. He preferred to imagine a garden, with Russian music growing alongside its neighbours.

For Tchaikovsky, music could belong to a wider European culture and still sound distinctly Russian. He heard French qualities in the music of Massenet and Bizet, just as Taneyev heard Russian qualities in Tchaikovsky’s compositions. Neither man was arguing that national character meant nothing. They disagreed about how it developed, and whether composers needed a deliberate programme of study to create it.

Tchaikovsky’s argument also had limitations. His letter dismissed English and Spanish music in terms that revealed his own prejudices. His garden was not a place where every tradition received equal admiration. Nevertheless, Tchaichovsky rejected the idea that Russian music needed to grow outside Europe. It had already taken root in shared musical ground.
Taneyev’s life shows how those connections worked in practice. In 1876, he reported playing Tchaikovsky’s piano concerto at the Paris home of the French composer Camille Saint-Saëns.

Tchaikovsky subsequently asked him to discuss a possible concert of his music in Paris. Taneyev would play the piano; French contacts would help make it happen. The plan came to nothing, but the correspondence shows musicians working across borders to find listeners.

The exchange was artistic as well as practical. Taneyev’s 1884 cantata John of Damascus, for choir and orchestra, draws on Russian sacred music while using the techniques he studied in earlier European works.

For listeners, the important point is that these influences could coexist. Learning from another tradition did not automatically make a composer’s music less connected to home. Calling Taneyev Russian remains useful. It connects him to the language, institutions and experiences that shaped his life. But it cannot explain his music on its own.
His career suggests that Russian classical music was never a closed national tradition. Even the ambition to create something distinctly Russian could depend on knowledge acquired from elsewhere.
That matters when composers become symbols of national identity today. Their music can express a sense of belonging while carrying the traces of other places, people and ideas.
Taneyev and Tchaikovsky disagreed about the best way forward. But argument points towards a shared lesson: that a national musical voice could emerge through international exchange.

articles.title: Clothes on the bed, nothing feels right: the psychology behind your seasonal wardrobe meltdown
articles.author: Catherine Greenwood, Lecturer in Digital Marketing, University of Lancashire
paras: The clocks have gone back, and suddenly getting dressed feels more difficult. The coat you wore constantly last winter is still hanging in the wardrobe, but it no longer looks quite how you remember. The boots you loved in February don’t seem to go with anything, while a jumper that once felt like you somehow doesn’t anymore.
Perhaps we’ve all simply forgotten how to dress for the cold. But there is something peculiar about returning to clothes we know so well and finding them unexpectedly unfamiliar.
As seasons change, we go back to garments we have worn before, but we don’t return to the same routines, experiences or even ways of feeling in our bodies. The seasons repeat, but our lives don’t.

In her 2007 book Why Women Wear What They Wear, anthropologist Sophie Woodward observed women choosing their clothes in the privacy of their bedrooms. She found that getting dressed was not simply about selecting an outfit. It involved negotiating how they wanted to look, what felt comfortable and how others might see them.

Woodward identified the importance of habitual clothing: garments we reach for regularly because we’ve learned how to wear them. By the end of summer, we know which trousers work with which shoes, how a dress moves and which combinations make us feel like ourselves. Those choices have become familiar through repetition.

Colder weather interrupts that familiarity. We bring back coats, tights, boots and layers, but they belong to combinations we haven’t practised for months. We may remember liking an outfit without immediately remembering how to inhabit it.
Our wardrobes hold more than clothes

Woodward’s research also helps us think about the different kinds of time contained within a wardrobe. Fashion operates through seasons, but our clothes accumulate across years, jobs, relationships and changing circumstances. A wardrobe can hold several periods of a life at once.

Clothing and textile expert Carole Hunt has researched the relationship between clothing and the past. She argues that textiles can act as carriers of knowledge and prompt recollection, sometimes through unexpected encounters. Think of pulling on a winter coat and finding an old train ticket in the pocket, or recognising the weight of a scarf you wore every day during a particular winter.

The garment does not have to be special to recall a time or place. Sometimes it is precisely the ordinary things we wore without thinking that become attached to our memories. This can make getting dressed feel unexpectedly difficult, particularly when clothes remind us of a time in our lives that feels different from the one we are living now.

But the transition to colder weather wardrobes is physical as well as emotional. Fashion sociologist Joanne Entwistle describes getting dressed as a “situated bodily practice”: this means clothing is experienced through both the body and the social circumstances in which we wear it.

Summer dressing can involve familiar sensations of bare ankles, lightweight fabric and uncovered arms. Winter asks us to adjust to the weight of coats, the restriction of layers, the feel of tights or the unfamiliar shape of boots. Even when an outfit looks right, it might not yet feel right.

The light has changed too. The clocks going back shift daylight within our daily routines, while the shortening days and lower winter sun change the settings in which we see ourselves. A familiar colour can appear different under a bedroom bulb from how it looks in the pale afternoon light. We are adjusting not only to wearing different clothes, but to seeing ourselves differently in them.

This need not amount to an identity crisis. It suggests something subtler: the confidence we associate with personal style may depend partly on repeated, ordinary encounters with our clothes. When those encounters change, familiarity has to be rebuilt.
Buying something new isn’t the answer

There is an irony in the fashion industry’s response to autumn. Each year, the season is presented as an invitation to start again, with new colours, silhouettes and supposedly essential purchases. Yet feeling uncertain about what to wear does not necessarily mean there is anything wrong with the clothes we already own.

Before deciding that last winter’s coat or favourite jumper no longer feels right, try it with something you regularly wear now, rather than attempting to recreate an outfit from the previous year. Taking photographs of different combinations can help you see possibilities you might otherwise overlook, although the real test is often wearing those clothes again. Something that feels unfamiliar in front of the mirror may feel quite different after an ordinary day spent wearing it.

This does not mean you should hold on to everything. Our tastes, circumstances and practical needs change, and some clothes may genuinely no longer have a place in your wardrobe. But there is a difference between a garment no longer being right and simply having forgotten what it feels like to wear it.

Perhaps that’s why the first cold weeks of autumn can feel so unsettling. We return to familiar clothes expecting to feel familiar ourselves, but personal style isn’t something we establish once and keep unchanged. It’s a relationship we continually remake with the things we wear.

articles.title: King Arthur and Ramayana: ancient stories that speak to the moral dilemmas of today’s leaders
articles.author: Harsh Trivedi, Teaching Associate French, School of Languages, Arts and Societies., University of Sheffield
paras: Across the vastly different worlds of ancient India and medieval Britain, two legendary rulers face the exact same impossible choice: sacrifice their love or shatter the moral foundation of their kingdom? It feels strikingly familiar in an era where modern heads of state are still forced to choose between personal loyalty and institutional justice.

The ancient Hindu epic Ramayana (attributed to Valmiki, 750-500BC) tells the story of Rama, prince and eventual king of Ayodhya, and his struggle to rescue his wife Sita after she is abducted by the demon-king Ravana. More than two millennia later, T.H. White’s The Once and Future King (1958) retells the Arthurian legend, his round table and the tragic love triangle between him, his queen, Guenever and the greatest knight of his realm, Lancelot.

Although separated by centuries, these two epics arrive at the same disturbing question: should the king let his queen burn? It is a dilemma that separates the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader.
This article is part of Rethinking the Classics. The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

After rescuing Sita and slaying Ravana, Rama initially rejects his wife. However privately certain he is of Sita’s loyalty, as a king, he must reckon with the public morality of his realm. Is a woman who has lived in another man’s captivity fit to be the queen? Furious, Sita demands a test by fire herself. She pleads with the god of fire not to let her burn if she has remained faithful to her husband and walks into the flames unscathed.

Queen Guenever, on the other hand, really is unfaithful to Arthur. As a husband, he has long made peace with her and Lancelot’s relationship, as he loves them both dearly. But when the other knights of Arthur’s court catch them red-handed in adultery, Arthur can no longer look away. As king, he is duty bound to submit to and uphold the public morality of his kingdom. He orders that Guenever be burnt at the stake. What makes the dilemma even greater for both kings is that both are bringers of a moral code to their respective realms.

Arthur dedicates his entire reign to implement his extraordinary political experiment of replacing “might” with “right”. He replaces brute force with a system of justice that binds even him. To this end, he creates his famous Round Table, recruiting knights who use their valour and strength to help the weak, thus transforming power from an instrument of oppression into that of law and order.
Rama too, is a great political innovator. Upon his ascension to the throne, he establishes Ram-Rajya – a utopian state of righteousness and equality before law.
When faced with the impossible choice between breaking moral codes or letting their queens burn, they decide to uphold the morality of their kingdoms at great personal cost.
It is of little consequence that Lancelot rescues Guenever and that fire itself refuses to burn Sita. Both kings must endure terrible suffering for their choice. T.H White’s Arthur laments:

What is right? […] What is wrong? If Lancelot does come to rescue her, he may kill those innocent fellows of the guard, which I have sent to burn her. They have trusted me and I have put them there to keep him off, because it is justice. If he saves her, they will be killed. If they are not killed, she will be burned. But burned to death, […], in horrible burning flames – and she is my much-loved Gwen.
Valmiki’s Rama is forced by the god of fire to justify himself not just to Sita but to the three worlds of the heavens, the earth and the netherworld. He pleads:

Before the three worlds, Sita needed to be purified. She had dwelt for a long period time in Ravana’s inner quarters. Had she not been purified, virtuous people would have told me that I am foolish and driven by desire. I know that Sita is single-mindedly devoted to me and that her mind is only on me. However, I am devoted to the truth.
Ultimately, Arthur’s “right” would have burnt Guenever alive were it not for the “might” of Lancelot. And it is precisely Rama’s Ram-Rajya that leads to the unfair treatment of Sita.

In both epics, paradoxically, good triumphs only when the prevailing moral order or justice system is defied. It is this inherent and underlying contradiction within both texts that makes them resonate with many of our very contemporary concerns.
When Joe Biden granted an “unconditional” presidential pardon to his son Hunter Biden for tax and gun-related offences in 2024, critics accused him of abusing public power to protect his own family.
Weeks later, on his first day back in office, Donald Trump granted sweeping clemency to nearly 1,600 people charged with or convicted of offences stemming from the January 6 Capitol attack.
The circumstances might be different, but the dilemma is very much the same that we find in Valmiki and T.H White’s texts: do our leaders have the right to a private morality?

It is their capacity to ask such profound and enduring questions that has kept both the Ramayana and the legend of King Arthur alive across centuries. Both stories have and will be retold by each generation and will continue to return as novels, films, TV series and graphic novels.

For anyone wishing to enter these wonderful worlds, my recommendation would be to begin with T. H. White’s The Once and Future King and Valmiki’s Ramayana, available in an excellent English translation by Bibek Debroy. Read together, they show why the epics still matter. They don’t give us easy answers, but they teach us how to ask better questions.

As part of the Rethinking the Classics series, we’re asking our experts to recommend a book or artwork that tackles similar themes to the canonical work in question, but isn’t (yet) considered a classic itself. Here is Harsh Trivedi’s suggestion:
May Our Joy Endure by Laura-Ève Lambert (2022) explores the moral contradictions of power through the character of Céline Wachowski.

Wachowski is a celebrated architect based in Montreal who gets “cancelled” following an exposé on the malpractices of her architectural firm. The novel explores a complex dilemma: can someone be both responsible for injustice and a victim of it?

Like Rama and Arthur, Wachowski finds herself caught between her personal convictions and the judgment of others. But unlike the two kings, who sacrifice their personal happiness in the name of public morality, Wachowski attempts to use her privilege to define what is right and influence the public narrative in her favour.

articles.title: Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery is a brilliant exploration of the life of the queen of crime
articles.author: Nadia Atia, Head of English & Reader in Postcolonial and Global Literature, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Coinciding with the 50th anniversary of Agatha Christie’s death, the exhibition A World of Mystery at the British Library takes visitors on a fascinating journey through spaces that evoke Christie’s life and work. This landmark exhibition offers unprecedented access to a body of private papers, diaries, manuscripts and family objects, brought together for public view for the first time.

Beautifully curated by Lucy Rowland, there is an impressive array of artefacts celebrating Christie’s life and work. Visitors can see objects that conjure important moments in Christie’s life from her Devon childhood to her travels around the globe, and her enormously successful career as novelist and playwright.

The exhibition begins in the English country house, a staple of Christie’s murder mysteries. Those less familiar with Christie’s biography will learn an enormous amount. But even die-hard fans will enjoy seeing hitherto closely guarded objects and manuscripts. There are rooms filled with childhood photographs, early stories written to impress her sister and hand-drawn sketches of St Mary Mead, Christie’s iconic English village and the setting for Miss Marple’s sleuthing. These sit alongside games that visitors can play and mysteries to be solved. For instance, what are your chances of being murdered in a Christie novel? Or, can you determine the motive behind the murder described?

In the exhibition’s second space, the dispensary, visitors learn not only about Christie’s war service and her training as a pharmaceutical dispenser, but how this specialist knowledge translated into murderous poisons used in her novels. Christie’s descriptions of poison were so detailed and accurate that they occasionally helped her readers to save lives.

Visitors are then transported to one of the most iconic of Christie’s spaces: the Orient Express. I have a longstanding interest in British travellers to Iraq in the early 20th century, which brought me to investigate Christie’s time in the country. I found the resonance of Christie’s travels to the Arab world beautifully evoked both in the Orient Express section and in the room that follows, dedicated to the archaeological dig.
Christie in the Middle East

As the exhibition describes, as a young woman, Christie was first taken to Cairo for her “coming out” – an opportunity for upper-class young women to be formally introduced into society. As Christie describes in her autobiography, “if you were well off, your mother gave a dance for you. You were supposed to go for a season in London”, but “there could be nothing like that in [Christie’s] life”. The Egyptian capital’s season was an affordable alternative to a traditional, expensive London coming out. Once there, she was not much interested in the city’s historical significance as a young girl, recalling: “The wonders of antiquity were the last thing I cared to see, and I am very glad [my mother] did not take me.”

She would return to the region in 1928 on a whim, changing her original plans to travel to the Caribbean at the last minute after a chance conversation inspired her to travel to the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, on the Orient Express instead. It was on that trip that she became friendly with the eminent archaeologist, Leonard Woolley, and his wife, Katharine, a fan of Christie’s writing.

Christie returned to Iraq to visit the couple at Ur (an ancient Sumerian city-state in southern Iraq) two years later. On that trip, she got to know Woolley’s assistant, Max Mallowan. As Mallowan describes in his memoir, Katharine urged the pair to take a trip together. As they took an impromptu swim in a saltwater lake, their car became stuck in the sand.

Mallowan describes how Christie’s stoic response to this minor disaster confirmed to him that “she must be a remarkable woman”. He proposed only a few months later, and the couple were married at St. Columba’s Church in Edinburgh in September 1930.

Throughout their married life, Christie accompanied Mallowan on almost all his excavations. The couple had a house in Baghdad and made temporary homes around the region. The exhibition highlights Christie’s often overlooked role on Mallowan’s digs.

She was a skilled photographer, supervised workmen on site, and cared for their finds, even using her moisturiser to clean ancient artefacts. It is surprisingly moving to see the small typewriter – cutting-edge technology in its day – which enabled Christie to live nomadically and write anywhere. She used it to draft some of her most famous novels.
Christie’s international reputation

The exhibition’s focus on space and place is mirrored in its investment in Christie as an author of global renown and influence. It underlines the ways in which Christie’s work – so often dismissed as lightweight, middlebrow, popular fiction – continues to circulate around the world in translation and adaption.

The more problematic aspects of Christie’s writing are also present. Attention is drawn to Christie’s antisemitism and her casual racism. The offensive original name of one of Christie’s most popular novels, And Then There Were None (1939) is never mentioned, but nevertheless it’s clear that the novel evolved and its title was changed in light of changing societal attitudes.

Before entering the exhibition proper, visitors pass a wall of Christie’s novels in translation. As we enjoy unauthorised Bollywood productions of And Then There Were None, posters advertising Shanghai productions of her play The Mousetrap, or interviews with Arab crime writers who reflect on Christie’s global literary legacy, there are continual reminders of the ways in which her writing has always appealed to worldwide audiences, despite the limitations that the exhibition highlights and critiques.

The final and most modern room is the theatre. Here, the visitor is transported to the West End. A large screen plays a black and white video of Christie, incredibly humble, celebrating the tenth anniversary of The Mouse Trap at the Savoy Hotel in London in 1962.

It’s difficult to overstate Christie’s modern legacy. Her work has been loved and emulated by millions. Electronic screens in the final rooms showcase that she has now sold over two billion novels; that she was the first woman to have two West End shows running at the same time; that there have been over 7,236 translations of her work.

Even 50 years after her death, she has sold 42,779 books worldwide just this week. Impressive, informative, but most of all great fun, Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery is a must see for anyone who has enjoyed Christie’s work.
Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery is at the British Library, London until June 20 2027

articles.title: Seeing is no longer believing: why physical witnesses matter more in the age of AI-generated content
articles.author: Oliver Bray, Dean of Leeds School of Arts, Leeds Beckett University
paras: When Elon Musk unveiled Tesla’s latest Roadster, much of the attention focused on the obvious spectacle. Here, apparently, was one of the oldest promises of science fiction finally made real: a flying car.

The demonstration had everything you might expect from contemporary technological theatre. Watching the futuristic vehicle on a looping track climb, flip and descend, it was difficult not to think of Hot Wheels tracks, science-fiction films and the illustrations of the future that filled children’s books during the latter half of the 20th century.

Yet what struck me most, as a researcher in performance and public communication, was not the car itself but the audience. The event was livestreamed, captured from multiple camera angles and quickly circulated online. People were also assembled to witness it physically. Most revealingly, Musk reportedly remarked that the live audience was there so nobody would think the footage had been made with AI. In a single sentence, he captured one of the defining cultural anxieties of the present moment: seeing is increasingly not enough when it comes to believing.

For more than a century, technologies of reproduction progressively reduced the importance of physical presence. In The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction, the cultural critic Walter Benjamin connected authenticity to an original’s particular “presence in time and space”. Photography allowed us to see somewhere we had not been, film extended that principle, television took it further and the internet collapsed geography altogether. For a time, the photograph or moving image acquired its own evidential authority: seeing something recorded was, with reasonable caveats, grounds for accepting that an event had occurred.

Artificial intelligence unsettles that relationship. Convincing images can now depict events that never happened. Deepfakes can simulate people saying things they never said. The significant change is that increasingly persuasive representations of reality need not have an originating event in the physical world.

This creates a curious reversal. The more sophisticated our technologies of representation become, the less the image alone can tell us about where it came from. In that context, the crowd at the Tesla demonstration acquires an unexpected function: they didn’t merely witness the evidence, they became a part of it. Audience members produced their own recordings and images, so credibility no longer rested entirely with Tesla’s official footage. The event acquired a form of distributed corroboration.

But there is an important problem here. Human witnesses are not reliable simply because they are human. When magician David Copperfield made the Statue of Liberty appear to disappear on television in April 1983, a live audience formed an essential part of the illusion. Around 50 million television viewers reportedly watched, but those physically present could truthfully say they had seen the statue apparently vanish – although it had, of course, gone nowhere. Copperfield’s audience didn’t authenticate an explanation of reality, it authenticated an experience.

So an event can be real, but witnesses do not always convert spectacle into truth. Audiences can be manipulated or incorporated into the performance they appear to authenticate. A hundred recordings of an illusion remain recordings of an illusion.
Perhaps the question then becomes not simply whether an image is real, but one about provenance. Where did that image come from and who is prepared to account for it?

Synthetic media (text, image, audio, video, or 3D assets that are artificially created, modified, or generated) doesn’t need a camera with an object in front of it, or even for a depicted scene to exist. This changes the nature of authenticity.

I have explored a related problem through the idea of the “unapproved orator”. Public communication increasingly reaches us through layers of speechwriting, editing, platforms, algorithms and summaries. The difficulty is not simply determining whether statements are true or false, but establishing whose voice we are really encountering and who ultimately stands behind it. Synthetic media pushes this further by allowing representations to circulate while their human origin, and therefore accountability, becomes increasingly difficult to establish.

A witness cannot resolve that problem. People can be wrong, lie or misunderstand what they have experienced. But a witness is present and can potentially be questioned. A witness can locate themselves within the event and say: “I was there”. In a sense, we borrow their presence. Perhaps that is what becomes valuable when images cease to function as reliable evidence alone. The question shifts from “does this look real?” to “where did this come from?” and “who stands behind it?”

For all its rockets, robots and flying cars, the technological future may therefore depend upon something extraordinarily old-fashioned: people gathering together, looking at something and afterwards being prepared to say, “I was there. I saw it happen.”

articles.title: Wild Horse Nine: Martin McDonagh’s odd-couple CIA drama is really a love story
articles.author: Andrew Dix, Senior Lecturer in American Literature and Film, Loughborough University
paras: “Is this a joke?” asks a young Chilean woman early in Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine. She is trying to grasp something said to her by another character; just as easily, however, she could be wondering exactly what kind of film she is in. For Wild Horse Nine itself is tonally unstable, mixing farcical events with historical drama and comic wordplay with an affecting portrait of male friendship.
This mixing of moods and blending of genres brings the film into alignment with McDonagh’s previous screen work as writer-director.

Beginning with In Bruges (2008) and continuing with Seven Psychopaths (2012), the Oscar-winning Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri (2017) and The Banshees of Inisherin (2022), McDonagh has always tried to disorient his audiences. A hitman may speak with unexpected profundity, say, or a moment of whimsical dialogue might give way to a scene of disturbing violence.

Wild Horse Nine follows other McDonagh projects, too, in its careful attention to time and place. The action occurs in 1973: first in a bleakly rendered Chile, just before the US-engineered coup that overthrew the socialist government of Salvador Allende; then in visually sumptuous Rapa Nui (Easter Island). Two CIA agents, Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell), travel to the island to play out a complicated personal and political endgame.

One of the film’s many pleasures is its detailed presentation of this island landscape (Wild Horse Nine is only the second film to have been shot there, following Kevin Reynolds’s historical epic Rapa-Nui in 1994).

Many of the 1,000 or so monolithic figures (the moai), fashioned by indigenous inhabitants between approximately 1400 and 1650, figure in key scenes. They evoke a sense of deep time against which the brief drama of these American incomers is unfolding.

McDonagh’s films have also been marked by their acute observation of men together. Consider in particular the complex bonds between the figures played by Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson in both In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin. Here, the Farrell character is revisited by Rockwell as Lee, while Gleeson’s part is taken by Malkovich as Chris.

The two men make for an odd couple. Physically, they exhibit a pleasing asymmetry: Lee the squatter and squishier of the two, sporting a moustache and often to be found with food in hand (or mouth). Chris, by contrast, is a grizzled presence, monumental and weather-worn like the moai in which he takes such pleasure.

Chris and Lee engage in rancorous verbal sparring. They differ as to how much discretion is expected of CIA operatives when in public. Yet their friendship has a weight and meaning, properly speaking a love, not replicated by any other interaction in their lives. Lee’s wife (Parker Posey), for example, is exploring adulterous options back in the US; while Chris’s brother (Tom Waits, in a delightful cameo), living in Monument Valley, Arizona, has all the gruffness of the cowboys who once rode that landscape.

Though male friendship is one of his thematic signatures, McDonagh senses a point of transition in his work with Wild Horse Nine. Perhaps, he recently mused to the Guardian, this is his first “old-man movie”. Thoughts of winding down, even termination, are spun through the film. As is characteristic of McDonagh’s cinema, however, melancholy is only one of its many moods, not a feeling that colours every shot.
If Wild Horse Nine is sensitive to place, it is equally scrupulous in recreating a particular point in time.

This is evident in the film’s visual texture, with saturated colours chosen to evoke the look of American cinema and photography in the early 1970s. Such care with history is apparent, too, in the narrative, as the personal drama of Chris and Lee occurs in sync with the crisis gathering in Chile.

There might be a temptation to downplay the film’s political engagement and prioritise instead its serious, though comic, personal drama, its exhilarating setting, its instances of zany Tarantino-esque dialogue (Chris musing, for example, on the logistics involved if a robin were to be a drug user). To set aside the politics, however, would be to impoverish the film.

From one perspective, it offers a cinematic version of “Greeneland”, to use the term devised for the territory explored by the mid-century English novelist Graham Greene. In globe-trotting fictions – including The Heart of the Matter (1948, set in Sierra Leone), The Quiet American (1955, Vietnam) and A Burnt-Out Case (1960, the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo) – Greene described ageing, depleted male characters reckoning with their guilt, particularly their role in advancing western imperialism.

Chris, in Wild Horse Nine, resembles one of Greene’s burnt-out cases. His energy is running down; memories of past CIA operations crowd his thoughts. It is further evidence of the film’s complexity that, prompted by his experiences on Rapa Nui, even this hardy agent of the American Empire comes to reflect on his being steeped in blood.

articles.title: Jonathan Swift foresaw the pitfalls of AI in Gulliver’s Travels
articles.author: Daniel Carey, Chair Professor School of English, Media and Creative Arts, University of Galway
paras: We think of artificial intelligence based on large language models as a discovery of our own moment. But Jonathan Swift – yes, the writer of Gulliver’s Travels (1726) – foresaw it all in the 18th century.
In our modern world we are repeatedly told by companies, governments, journalists and others that our lives can be changed through the assistance of AI.

By plugging our questions into a machine and assigning it tasks of composition (from reports to books, essays, letters and even creative writing) we can sit back and let ChatGPT and its rivals do the work. Remarkable gains in knowledge and productivity are promised, based on an obscure internal architecture of algorithms that beaver away on our requests. Swift was wise to these ambitions and cast a sceptical eye on their claims.

Gulliver’s Travels, his greatest satirical achievement, covers enormous ground in the objects it submits to scrutiny. The first two trips famously lead to his encounter with the petty little Lilliputians and the outsize Brobdingnagians who expose the hero to various indignities and examinations that call his assumptions into question. In his fourth and final journey, the noble Houyhnhnms – rational horses with the gift of speech – emerge as paragons for Gulliver that make him doubt the value of humanity.

His third voyage, however, receives much less attention and forms no part of the popular recollection of what happens to him across his travels. Yet this sequence contains a multitude of instructive satirical occasions, one of which we could see as anticipating AI.

During his visit to the learned Academy of Lagado (situated in the metropolis of the country of Balnibarbi), Gulliver makes contact with a group of “projectors”. This cohort of thinkers, through extravagant schemes, anticipate that their efforts will achieve great breakthroughs in practical and theoretical knowledge. It is largely held that Swift’s real world target here was the Royal Society of London and its cadre of experimenting scientists.

Swift has Gulliver introduced to an array of projects. The first series includes a number of practical attempts to harness nature. For instance, by extracting sunbeams from cucumbers and reducing excrement to its original food, among other ludicrous endeavours.
Then we come to the side of the Academy where plans to advance speculative learning take place. Here is the point at which AI comes into view.

Gulliver informs us that he entered a large room where a professor was at work on a project with 40 assistants. He sees a large frame occupying most of the space. This device, we learn, has the function of relieving the labour involved in attaining breakthroughs in arts and science.

Happily, the device solves the problem, ensuring that “the most ignorant person” could, by using this tool, “write Books in Philosophy, Poetry, Politicks, Law, Mathematics and Theology” without possessing any genius or engaging in any study.

Gulliver describes in detail the appearance of the apparatus, constructed on a 20 ft by 20 ft frame with a series of 40 handles or cranks around it. The device features a series of small blocks of wood about the size of dice, linked by a number of wires. Each block is covered by a pasted piece of paper with a word of the local language written on it.

Gulliver gets treated to a demonstration. On the order of the project lead, the assistants turn the iron handles, changing the whole relationship and sequence of words on the dice. The assistants then read out the combinations, with scribes taking down any intelligible sequences, a process repeated six hours a day.

The proud professor shows Gulliver a number of volumes in folio produced by this method, consisting of broken sentences that he plans to piece together. Out of these “rich materials” he promises “a compleat Body of all Arts and Sciences”. All that was needed was sufficient funding and the provision of 500 additional frames to amass their many findings.

Here, I submit, we have an outline of AI – at least in its LLM (large language model) incarnation. The LLM here has been put in place, admittedly with a cumbersome system of word combinations and the distant prospect of coherence. The key is that the machine does the work and a system, however imperfect, mechanically operates on language to produce its results. Here too is the promise of infinite progress in intelligence conferred on any operator, however ignorant (Swift is, after all, a satirist).

What Swift misses out, it must be said, is the refinement of enabling individual users to ask the machine a specific question. But that is only part of AI of course. Much of it is “content generation” unprompted by questions, simply the application of tools to a corpus of accumulated words to generate new material, in the manner of the Lagado experiment.

Swift shows us the technical approach, and above all the labour-saving premise of the operation. By implication, the contraption produces plenty of gibberish from random collisions of language (weeded out by scribes), with the whole process redeemed when it magically produces something meaningful.

The nub of Swift’s critique is his exposure of the illusion that strings of machine-generated text will compose themselves into intelligible and instructive tomes of philosophy, poetry, theology, etc. We have made substantial progress beyond this hand-cranked approach put forward by the Lagado academicians, but the passive model of intelligence that underpins it is the same. Arguably we lack the one caution they impose, in having checkers at the ready to do some sifting. We have no such provision for inhibiting AI hallucinations.

Gulliver concludes his account by saying he thanked the illustrious professor for his demonstration and promised to credit him with its invention. Perhaps we should thank Swift for anticipating AI and drawing attention to its limitations.

articles.title: Four foods with ancient roots that we still eat on Bonfire Night
articles.author: Pippa Catterall, Professor of History and Policy, University of Westminster
paras: The gunpowder plot of 1605 was an attempt to assassinate King James I, blow up London’s Houses of Parliament and trigger a full-scale Catholic rebellion in England. To commemorate its spectacular failure, parliament passed the Act for a Public Thanksgiving to Almighty God Every Year on the Fifth Day of November. But few needed an excuse for celebrations as winter closed in.

In Jacobean England, November 5 added just another red-letter day to a calendar already enlivened by the bonfires lit in commemoration of Elizabeth I’s accession on November 17. But the English tradition of bonfires and feasting didn’t begin with Elizabeth either. The ritualised burning of the debris of the year can be dated back to pre-Christian times. The act of 1605 both sanctioned and positively encouraged such activities.
Food was always an important part of the merrymaking. Here are four of the most popular delicacies that have marked bonfire season in England over the centuries.

As a child in the 1960s, I remember my mother wrapping potatoes in tinfoil to stick on the edge of a roaring fire to bake. Afterwards, in keeping with traditions in her native Lancashire, there would be parkin (a dense gingerbread cake) and tray-baked homemade treacle toffee that you had to hammer to break up. In village firework parties in the north of England, such food traditions are still going strong.

Interestingly, tossing them in the embers is mentioned in the first British reference to potatoes in a herbal (a guide to plants and herbs) by John Gerard, published in 1633. This was apparently seen as a way of making them “lose much of their windinesse, especially being eaten sopped in wine”.

Potatoes, albeit generally smaller and in fewer varieties than available today, were first introduced in England in the 1570s. Acceptance was remarkably slow. Long dismissed as an exotic novelty or livestock feed, they only became a mainstream English staple during the food shortages of the late 18th century. Yet as Gerard’s 1633 account proves, early adopters had already figured out that the embers of a fire were the easiest way to bake them.
Maybe the tradition of sopping them in wine continues today in the peculiar British tradition of putting vinegar on chips.

Parkin, however, is of more recent origin. The first recorded reference to it is seemingly when a woman named Sarah Priestley was arraigned at Pontefract Quarter Sessions in 1729 for stealing oatmeal to make a parkin. This clearly indicates that parkin was already a desirable Yorkshire delicacy, but leaves its origins obscure.

Parkin seems to have evolved from “tharf cakes”, large round oaten cakes, sometimes made with plums inside. They are recorded as far back as the Lindisfarne gospels, a Christian manuscript created around AD700-715. Tharf cakes were a 12th night delicacy in Cumbria and a November 5 tradition in Sheffield up to the late 19th century.

Eighteenth-century parkin, like tharf cakes, was a thin oatmeal cake baked directly on a griddle stone. What made it parkin was the addition of ginger and a sweetener. Depending on region this is generally black treacle (Yorkshire), syrup (Lancashire) or even honey (West Yorkshire).
From the mid-19th century, parkin began to be commercially produced in ovens with bicarbonate of soda added to leaven it and give it what has become its characteristic texture.
The production of parkin drew on the surplus of oats at the end of the harvest. As oats were not generally grown in the south of England, its consumption never caught on there.
In most parts of England, it is likely that the first sweetmeats associated with November 5 were soul cakes. These are small, round cakes flavoured with spices such as nutmeg and ginger.

According to T. F. Thistleton-Dyer’s book British Popular Customs (1876), the custom of going “a-souling” – begging or singing for soul cakes – was already well established by Shakespeare’s time, as a pastime during the celebrations of All Hallowstide between October 31 and November 2.
Indeed, this tradition goes back further, as an appropriation of the Celtic tradition of Samhain and is the distant origin of modern trick or treating at Halloween.

The tradition of seeking cakes “or any good thing to make them merry” was easily adapted to Bonfire Night from 1605. This included seasonal fruits. For instance, in Cheshire, one of the songs associated with the season emphasised “we are come for apples and strong beer”.

Apples and sweetmeats therefore became adopted as part of the fun on the new festive date of November 5 after 1605. Eventually, the two were put together. From the 1890s, toffee apples began to appear in London during these festivities.

These foods are all part of the historic experience of Bonfire Night and the smells and tastes it evokes. The festivities would not be the same without the food associated with it. Indeed, the idea that the distinctive nature and flavour of regional foods need to be protected is even enshrined in European law.

When Britain was in the EU, foodstuffs such as Melton Mowbray pies, stilton cheese and Cornish pasties were given this protected status. This continues under post-Brexit arrangements. Yet this list of protected foodstuffs does not, as yet, include parkin. Maybe it should. After all, in the north of England parkin is an important – and delicious – part of the intangible cultural heritage of Guy Fawkes Day.
